lessons.title: Event Loop, Promises, and Asynchronous Work
lessons.summary: JavaScript can start asynchronous operations while the runtime continues processing other work.
lessons.body:
Event Loop, Promises, and Asynchronous Work

Why this matters
JavaScript can start asynchronous operations while the runtime continues processing other work. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• JavaScript can start asynchronous operations while the runtime continues processing other work.
• A Promise represents eventual fulfillment or rejection, not a background thread you control directly.
• Microtasks/callback scheduling explains why logs can appear in an order different from source lines.
• Reason about when a value exists rather than treating async/await as syntax magic.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, javascript foundations ii: async and http stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter event loop, promises, and asynchronous work again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

lessons.title: async/await and Error Propagation
lessons.summary: An async function always returns a Promise.
lessons.body:
async/await and Error Propagation

Why this matters
An async function always returns a Promise. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• An async function always returns a Promise.
• await pauses that async function until the awaited Promise settles; it does not block the entire server/browser runtime.
• Rejected Promises propagate like thrown errors through async functions until handled.
• Use try/catch when you can recover/map/add context, not merely to print and continue with invalid state.

lessons.title: Fetch and HTTP from JavaScript
lessons.summary: fetch resolves for HTTP error statuses such as 404/500; code must inspect response.ok/status.
lessons.body:
Fetch and HTTP from JavaScript

Why this matters
fetch resolves for HTTP error statuses such as 404/500; code must inspect response.ok/status. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

lessons.title: Concurrency, Race Conditions, and Stale Results
lessons.summary: Two requests can finish in a different order from which they started.
lessons.body:
Concurrency, Race Conditions, and Stale Results

Why this matters
Two requests can finish in a different order from which they started. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Two requests can finish in a different order from which they started.
• A stale response can overwrite newer user intent if code does not track identity/version/cancellation.
• Promise.all is useful when operations are independent and all must succeed; sequential await is appropriate when later work depends on earlier results.
• Optimistic updates and realtime later make race reasoning even more important.

lessons.summary: Separate network failure, HTTP failure, parse failure, validation failure, and business failure.
lessons.body:
Debugging Async and Network Failures

Why this matters
Separate network failure, HTTP failure, parse failure, validation failure, and business failure. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Separate network failure, HTTP failure, parse failure, validation failure, and business failure.
• Use Network timing/status/body and server logs together instead of relying on one console message.
• Record request identifiers when systems span multiple processes.
• Reproduce with curl/API client to determine whether the UI is involved.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, javascript foundations ii: async and http stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter debugging async and network failures again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

lessons.body:
Lab: Debugging Async and Network Failures

Purpose
This lab converts the previous explanation into a small piece of evidence you created yourself. Do not begin by copying the finished example. Start with the behavior you expect, then make the computer prove or disprove your model.

Your task
Build the smallest runnable example for “Debugging Async and Network Failures”, predict its output, change one assumption, and explain the difference using concrete evidence.

Working method
1. Create the smallest clean starting point.
2. Predict the first result in writing.
3. Implement only enough to test that prediction.
4. Run it and capture the result.
5. Add one intentional failure or changed assumption.
6. Diagnose from evidence before editing randomly.
7. Restore the correct behavior.
8. Close the reference and reproduce the important part from memory.

Why this is separate from the concept lesson
Reading can create familiarity without recall. The separate lab forces retrieval, execution, and debugging. Those three abilities are what later framework lessons assume when the codebase becomes larger.

Definition of done
You have a runnable example, one recorded prediction, one successful result, one controlled failure with diagnosis, and a short explain-back in your own words.
